name: autogen

facts.description: A programming framework for agentic AI

title: AutoGen: A Python Framework for Agentic AI
answer: AutoGen is a Python programming framework for agentic AI, created by Microsoft. It lets you build applications where multiple LLM-backed agents converse, use tools, and execute code to solve tasks. It sits at the orchestration layer, above raw model APIs and below your application. The one thing to know: it is powerful for multi-agent workflows but requires careful configuration, and its 0.2 to 0.4 migration means older examples may not run unchanged.

sections.body: AutoGen is a programming framework for agentic AI, made by Microsoft and distributed as an open-source Python package under the CC-BY-4.0 licence. The repository is microsoft/autogen, and the official site is microsoft.github.io/autogen. It first appeared publicly in 2023, and by April 2026 the repository had accumulated over 61,000 stars. It occupies the orchestration layer of the AI stack: it does not train models or serve them at scale, but coordinates calls to large language models, manages conversation state, executes generated code, and lets multiple agents collaborate on a task. In practice it sits between a model provider such as OpenAI or a local endpoint and the application logic you write.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is used for multi-agent conversation, tool use, code execution, and enhanced inference. Documented use cases include MathChat, a conversational pattern for advanced mathematics where a user proxy agent and an LLM assistant collaborate, and AutoDefense, a multi-agent defense that filters harmful model responses using intention analysis, prompt inferring, and a final judgment. It also supports local inference through OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as FastChat with ChatGLM2-6B, and enhanced inference features including caching, error handling, multi-config inference, result filtering, and templating. It is strongest when a task benefits from several specialized agents, each with a focused role, rather than a single prompt.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: AutoGen assumes working Python knowledge, and the official material is written for developers rather than absolute beginners. You need to understand how to call an LLM API, how to configure model endpoints, and how to handle asynchronous or multi-step programs. Some examples, such as MathChat, involve mathematical problem solving, but the framework itself does not demand advanced mathematics. The official site offers a blog, documentation pages, and migration guides, including a guide for moving from 0.2 to 0.4. The learning curve is moderate: simple two-agent conversations are quick to build, while production patterns with custom agents, tool use, and observability take longer to master.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: AutoGen has a substantial ecosystem. The official site documents integrations with AgentOps, described as its official agent observability tool, which provides monitoring of LLM calls, costs, latency, agent failures, multi-agent interactions, and tool usage from one dashboard, and which can be enabled with an API key and a call to agentops.init(). The framework works with OpenAI and Azure OpenAI endpoints, with custom endpoints such as llama-7B, and with local models served through FastChat. It offers autogen.OpenAIWrapper for openai>=1 and autogen.Completion as a drop-in replacement for older OpenAI clients. The project states it is the official project and is not affiliated with any forks or startups. Community support is visible through the repository, blog posts, and research examples such as AutoDefense.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: AutoGen is built for both quick experiments and production use, though the balance depends on how you configure it. A basic two-agent conversation can be written in a few lines, which makes prototyping fast. For production, the framework offers caching, error handling, multi-config inference with fallback across models, result filtering, and observability through AgentOps. The cost is configuration complexity: llm_config must be set correctly, deepcopy behaviour can cause errors with objects that do not support it, and the 0.2 to 0.4 migration means older code may need changes. The official material does not claim that AutoGen itself optimizes model speed or memory; those remain properties of the underlying model and serving stack.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: AutoGen is a current and widely used framework, not a legacy choice. Its repository has over 61,000 stars, it is maintained by Microsoft, and the official site documents enterprise-oriented features such as AgentOps monitoring and compliance. The blog notes that Bloomberg declared 2024 the year of AI agents, and AutoGen positions itself as a tool for building enterprise-grade agents. For someone choosing what to learn, AutoGen is a reasonable investment for roles involving agent orchestration, multi-agent systems, and LLM application development. The facts and the site do not name specific companies using it in production beyond Microsoft and the AgentOps partnership, so claims about broad industry deployment should be treated cautiously.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: AutoGen is a Python framework, and it is typically used alongside the OpenAI Python client, FastChat for local model serving, and HuggingFace Hub for downloading model checkpoints. It can call models through OpenAI-compatible APIs, which makes it a drop-in replacement in some setups, and it supports Azure OpenAI with deployment names and API versions. It belongs to the polyglot pattern where Python handles orchestration and model interaction while other languages or services handle data storage, web serving, or user interfaces. The official site does not document first-class bindings for other languages, so teams working in Java, Go, or JavaScript would typically call AutoGen-based services over a network rather than embed the framework directly.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: AutoGen is not a model training or serving framework, and it does not manage GPU memory or inference speed. Its multi-agent patterns can be harder to debug than single-agent code, which is why observability tools such as AgentOps are promoted. The 0.2 to 0.4 transition is a real cost, since examples and APIs differ between versions. The official material does not specify benchmark performance against other agent frameworks, does not give a detailed security model beyond the AutoDefense research example, and does not state how many production deployments exist. Questions about long-term API stability, the exact scope of the CC-BY-4.0 licence for code versus documentation, and support for non-Python environments remain unsettled by the pages read.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
